nameStory: This tiny bee gets its 'mock-orange' name from its strong preference for visiting mock-orange flowers (Philadelphus species), where it was first discovered and studied. The 'scissor bee' part comes from the way these bees use their scissor-like jaws to cut and shape materials for their nests, snipping pieces with precise movements like tiny garden shears.
description: The Mock-orange Scissor Bee is a small, dark solitary bee that specializes in visiting white, fragrant flowers. These bees are much smaller than honeybees, with slender bodies that appear almost black with subtle metallic hints. Unlike social bees that live in hives, scissor bees are solitary, with each female building her own individual nest. They're part of the mason bee family, known for their skilled construction abilities using natural materials.

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Very small and slender, noticeably smaller than a honeybee with a narrow waist and elongated body that looks almost stick-like when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Flower Preference
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on white, cup-shaped flowers, especially mock-orange shrubs where they dive deep into blooms and emerge dusted with white pollen

idTips.label: Body Color
idTips.description: Dark blackish-brown body with a subtle metallic sheen that catches the light, lacking the fuzzy appearance of bumblebees or the golden tones of honeybees

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Quick, darting flight between flowers with frequent hovering, moving in short bursts rather than the steady flight of larger bees

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Solitary behavior with no workers or guards around, often seen alone or just a few individuals per flowering shrub

habitat: Found in gardens, parks, and woodland edges where mock-orange and other white-flowered shrubs grow, particularly in suburban and semi-urban areas. They prefer sunny to partially shaded locations with well-established ornamental plantings. Look for them in botanical gardens, older residential neighborhoods, and campus settings where mock-orange shrubs are commonly planted.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring as mock-orange buds start to swell, with peak activity coinciding with mock-orange bloom time in May and early June.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when mock-orange and other white flowers are in full bloom. Females are busy collecting pollen and building nests in early to mid-summer.
seasonality.fall: Adults have finished their lifecycle and are no longer visible. Next generation is developing in nest cavities as larvae.
seasonality.winter: Overwintering as larvae or pupae in their nest cavities, completely hidden from view until the following spring emergence.

funFact: These bees are so specialized that they can identify their preferred flowers by scent alone from over 100 feet away, and will fly past dozens of other perfectly good flowers to reach a single mock-orange bloom, making them like tiny floral sommeliers with incredibly refined taste.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with small dark sweat bees, but scissor bees are much more slender and stick-like, while sweat bees are more compact and rounded. Remember: if it's long and skinny on white flowers, think scissor; if it's small and chunky, think sweat bee.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'mock-orange,' these bees don't actually visit citrus orange trees - the mock-orange plant (Philadelphus) is named for its orange-blossom-like fragrance but is completely unrelated to citrus fruits, belonging instead to the hydrangea family.
compareHints: The Mock-orange Scissor Bee is extremely similar to the Rampion Scissor Bee, but they can be distinguished by their flower preferences - Mock-orange Scissor Bees stick almost exclusively to white flowers like mock-orange, while Rampion Scissor Bees prefer blue bell-shaped flowers. Both are small and dark, but their habitat choices make identification easier than trying to spot physical differences.
